excerpt: An intoxicated pedestrian can still recover in Georgia and South Carolina. How shared fault is assessed, and what it costs a claim.
keyTakeaways: Intoxicated pedestrians can file personal injury claims in both Georgia and South Carolina under modified comparative fault rules. Georgia allows recovery if less than 50% at fault (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33); South Carolina if less than 51% (Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co.). Drivers owe a duty of care to all pedestrians, and both states' statutes expressly require extra precaution around an obviously intoxicated person (O.C.G.A. § 40-6-93; S.C. Code § 56-5-3230). Compensation is reduced proportionally to fault percentage. Georgia has a 2-year statute of limitations (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33); South Carolina has 3 years (S.C. Code § 15-3-530).

faqs.question: Can I file a personal injury claim if I was drunk when hit by a car?
faqs.answer: Yes. In both Georgia and South Carolina, being intoxicated does not automatically bar you from filing a personal injury claim. Both states follow comparative fault systems that allow recovery as long as your share of fault is below the state threshold — less than 50% in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33) and less than 51% in South Carolina (Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co.).

faqs.question: How does being intoxicated affect my compensation?
faqs.answer: Your intoxication may increase your assigned percentage of fault, which reduces your compensation proportionally. For example, if you are found 30% at fault due to intoxication and your damages total $200,000, you would recover $140,000. However, if your fault reaches the state threshold, you receive nothing.

faqs.question: Does a driver have a duty to avoid hitting a drunk pedestrian?
faqs.answer: Yes. In both Georgia and South Carolina, drivers must exercise due care to avoid colliding with any pedestrian. Both states' due-care statutes specifically require drivers to take proper precautions upon observing any child or any obviously confused, incapacitated, or intoxicated person (O.C.G.A. § 40-6-93; S.C. Code § 56-5-3230). A driver who was speeding, texting, or otherwise negligent can still be held liable even if the pedestrian was intoxicated — the pedestrian's share of fault reduces the award rather than erasing the claim, unless it reaches the state's bar.

faqs.question: What is the statute of limitations for a pedestrian accident claim?
faqs.answer: In Georgia, you have 2 years from the date of the accident to file a lawsuit (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33). In South Carolina, you have 3 years (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). Missing these deadlines means losing your right to sue.

faqs.question: Will the insurance company deny my claim because I was drinking?
faqs.answer: Insurance companies will try to use your intoxication to minimize or deny your claim, but drinking alone does not bar recovery in either state — if the driver was negligent, a denial can be challenged by filing suit against the driver. They may argue higher fault percentages or use tactics like requesting recorded statements. Having an attorney handle communications protects your rights.

faqs.question: What evidence helps prove a pedestrian accident claim when the pedestrian was intoxicated?
faqs.answer: Key evidence includes surveillance camera footage, witness testimony, the police report, the driver's cell phone records showing distraction, accident reconstruction analysis, and vehicle black box data showing speed and braking. This evidence helps establish driver negligence independent of the pedestrian's intoxication.
